<reason>Both sides ran disciplined, comparative cases and the clash narrowed properly across rounds. CON's strongest move was reframing PRO's stigma/paperwork case as an indictment of bad means testing, then offering data-matched and building-level targeting as capturing the dignity benefits without subsidising affluent families; its "food isn't a fixed cost" hit on PRO's cafeteria economics was clean. But CON's decisive premise — that universal trays cannibalise backpack/breakfast money for the neediest — never got grounded. PRO's Q2 demanded the redirection rule, and CON's answer (anti-hunger money is a protected statutory line item) is in tension with its own crowd-out story and with its earlier claim that targeted subsidies survive austerity. PRO also extracted a real concession under pressure: CON admitted the "remaining sliver" of children (just above SNAP, unenrolled, undocumented, in low-poverty buildings) is "a real design problem," and PRO's closing correctly weighed that as a child waiting on a promised redesign. PRO's error-asymmetry frame (a missed hungry child versus a wealthy family recovering a fraction of its own taxes), plus the sharp observation that CON's two-tier model still requires balances, debt-chasing and reconciliation ("the doctor's son isn't the beneficiary; he's the seam it removes"), gave the cleaner voting reason. CON also slightly mischaracterised PRO's rebuttal as PRO "proposing" building-level meals, and had two clipped speeches to PRO's one. Close but PRO built the more secure route.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Q1 and follow-up: pressing who feeds the child just above the SNAP line, unenrolled, or avoiding government rolls forced CON to concede the "remaining sliver is a real design problem," which PRO then converted into its central error-asymmetry weighing. Paired with PRO's demand for the mechanism guaranteeing that money not spent on middle-income students actually reaches backpack programs, it left CON's fixed-pot crowd-out claim unsecured.</best_rebuttal>
